entries.original: If $M$ has socle length $n$ (i.e., $Soc^n (M) = M$ but $Soc^(n-1)(M) != M$) then $M$ also has radical length $n$
entries.corrected: If $M$ has a composition series and socle length $n$ (i.e., $Soc^n (M) = M$ but $Soc^(n-1)(M) != M$) then $M$ also has radical length $n$
entries.reason: For an arbitrary module only $Rad^n (M) = 0$ and the inclusions $Soc^j (M) supset.eq Rad^(n-j)(M)$ follow; the two lengths can differ. For the ring $Lambda$ of eventually constant sequences over a field and $M = lmodule(Lambda, Lambda)$ we have $Rad(M) = J(Lambda) = 0$ (radical length 1), while $Soc(M)$ consists of the sequences of finite support and $M slash Soc(M)$ is simple (socle length 2). For modules of finite length the two lengths agree.
entries.verified_by: M. Linckelmann, The Block Theory of Finite Group Algebras, Vol. I (2018), Section 1.10: the paragraph before Theorem 1.10.22 and Theorem 1.10.22 (iii); P. Webb, A Course in Finite Group Representation Theory (2016), Proposition 6.3.8; checks/sage/chapter-1.py, section_1_2 (the corrected statement on 142 modules of 16 algebras).

entries.original: It is a two sided ideal $I$ which is *primitive*, meaning that $Lambda slash I$ has a faithful irreducible module.
entries.corrected: It is a two sided ideal $I$. If $M$ is irreducible then $I$ is *primitive*, meaning that $Lambda slash I$ has a faithful irreducible module.
entries.reason: The annihilator of a module need not be primitive: for $Lambda = ZZ$ and $M = ZZ$ it is $0$, and $ZZ$ has no faithful irreducible module (the irreducible $ZZ$-modules $ZZ slash p ZZ$ are annihilated by $p$). If $M$ is irreducible, it is a faithful irreducible $Lambda slash I$-module; these are the primitive ideals whose intersection is $J(Lambda)$ in the next sentence.
entries.verified_by: T. Y. Lam, A First Course in Noncommutative Rings, 2nd ed. (2001), Definitions (11.2), (11.3), Proposition (11.4) and Corollary (11.5), pp. 195-196; checks/sage/chapter-1.py, section_1_2.

entries.original: Then a $k Q$-module is the same thing as a chain complex of vector spaces. The projective $k Q$-modules are the exact complexes. ... and a $Lambda Q$-module is the same as a chain complex of $Lambda$-modules. The projective $Lambda Q$-modules are the split exact sequences of projective $Lambda$-modules.
entries.corrected: Then a $k Q slash I$-module is the same thing as a chain complex of vector spaces. entries.reason: The relations $I$ make the composite of two consecutive maps zero; the algebra of the quiver with relations is $k Q slash I$ (Definition 4.1.8). Likewise for $Lambda Q$, with $I$ the ideal of the paths of length at least two.

entries.place: Proof of Theorem 4.3.2, last two sentences
entries.original: But a row vector $(u_11, dots, u_(n m))$ annihilated by this matrix gives rise to a vector $v'(lambda)$ of degree $(n - 1)$ in $lambda$ satisfying $v'(lambda)(A' + lambda B') = 0$. Thus $(0, v'(lambda)) mat(E_lambda (n), C + lambda D; 0, A' + lambda B') = 0$ and so there is also a column vector of degree $(n - 1)$ in $lambda$ annihilated by $a + lambda b$, contradicting the minimality of $n$.
entries.corrected: But a column vector annihilated by this matrix gives a vector $u(lambda)$ of degree at most $n - 2$ with $(A' + lambda B') u(lambda) = 0$; since $E_lambda (n)$ maps the vectors of degree at most $n - 1$ bijectively onto those of degree at most $n$, there is $w(lambda)$ of degree at most $n - 1$ with $E_lambda (n) w(lambda) = -(C + lambda D) u(lambda)$, and $(w(lambda), u(lambda))$ is a column vector of degree at most $n - 1$ annihilated by $a + lambda b$, contradicting the minimality of $n$.
entries.reason: A row vector annihilated by the matrix always exists, since it has more rows than columns, and it gives no column vector annihilated by $a + lambda b$; the full column rank needs a column vector.
entries.verified_by: checks/sage/chapter-4a.py, proof of Theorem 4.3.2 (the corrected last step); Simson and Skowroński, Elements of the representation theory of associative algebras, vol. 2 (2007), Theorem XI.4.6.
